lessons.title: Work, energy and power
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Physics — Work, energy, power, simple machines (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate work done, kinetic energy and potential energy.
State the principle of conservation of energy and apply it to a falling object.
reviewNotes: g = 10 N/kg is used; efficiency and machines follow in the next lesson.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Work and power
blocks.md: **Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force**, **W = F × d**. The unit is the **joule (J)**: 1 J = 1 N m. **Power** is the rate of doing work: **P = W ÷ t**, unit the **watt (W)** = 1 J/s. A 100 W bulb transfers 100 J of energy each second.

blocks.title: Kinetic and potential energy
blocks.md: **Kinetic energy** (moving): **KE = ½ m v²**. **Gravitational potential energy** (height): **PE = m g h** (g = 10 N/kg). Energy is measured in joules. Doing work on an object transfers energy to it: work done = energy transferred.

blocks.caption: A 2 kg ball dropped from 5 m: potential energy changes to kinetic energy (joules).
blocks.alt: A bar chart: potential energy 100 J at the top and 50 J half-way, kinetic energy 50 J half-way and 100 J at the end.

blocks.title: Conservation of energy
blocks.md: Energy is **never created or destroyed**, only changed from one form to another: **the total energy stays the same** (when no energy is lost as heat by friction). For a ball falling freely, PE lost = KE gained: **m g h = ½ m v²**, so **v = √(2 g h)**. Some energy is always spread as heat, which is why machines are less than 100 % efficient.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- No work is done if there is no movement, e.g. pushing a wall that does not move.
- Use the weight (N), not the mass, in W = F × d when lifting; weight = m × 10.
- In KE = ½ m v² the speed is **squared**: doubling the speed multiplies KE by 4.

blocks.title: Work and power in lifting
blocks.statement: A porter lifts a 50 kg bag steadily through 2 m in 5 s (g = 10 N/kg). Find the work done and the power.

blocks.title: Speed of a falling ball
blocks.statement: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 5 m. Find its speed just before it hits the ground (ignore air resistance).
steps: PE at the top = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J, all becomes KE: ½ × 2 × v² = 100.

lessons.title: Simple machines and efficiency
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Physics — Work, energy, power, simple machines (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define a machine, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency.
Name the three classes of lever and give an example of each.
Calculate MA, VR and efficiency for levers, pulleys and inclined planes.
reviewNotes: For pulley systems VR = number of supporting ropes (ideal model); check the syllabus definition of efficiency (output/input work).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Machines
blocks.md: A **machine** makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force (it does not give extra energy). Simple machines: **lever**, **pulley**, **inclined plane (ramp)**, **wheel and axle**, **screw**, **wedge**. The **load** is the force to overcome and the **effort** is the force applied.

blocks.caption: A lever: load and effort on either side of the pivot.
blocks.alt: A beam on a pivot with a load arrow downward on the left and an effort arrow downward on the right.

blocks.title: MA, VR and efficiency
blocks.md: **Mechanical advantage MA = load ÷ effort** (no unit). **Velocity ratio VR = distance moved by the effort ÷ distance moved by the load** (for a ramp: length of the slope ÷ height; for a pulley system: the number of supporting ropes). **Efficiency = (work output ÷ work input) × 100 % = (MA ÷ VR) × 100 %**. Efficiency is always **below 100 %** because of friction.

blocks.title: Classes of lever
blocks.md: **Class 1**: pivot between load and effort (seesaw, scissors, crowbar). **Class 2**: load between pivot and effort (wheelbarrow, nutcracker). **Class 3**: effort between pivot and load (tweezers, a person's forearm, fishing rod). Class 2 levers always have MA greater than 1; class 3 levers have MA less than 1 but give speed and range.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A machine cannot have an efficiency over 100 %: that would create energy.
- MA has **no unit**; VR also has none.
- A big MA means a small effort but a **long** distance for the effort.

blocks.title: Pulley system
blocks.statement: A pulley system with 4 supporting ropes raises a 400 N load with an effort of 150 N. Find MA, VR and the efficiency.

blocks.title: Ramp
blocks.statement: A 600 N barrel is pushed up a ramp 3 m long and 1 m high with an effort of 300 N. Find MA, VR and efficiency.
